headline: WHEAT AND BEANS CLOSE THE WEEK STRONG
subheadline: Friday's close had wheat up nearly 3% and soybeans at a 52-week high, while corn sat out; the September WASDE is now the market's next hard test.
lead: Wheat finished Friday at $7.66, up 21 cents on the session, and soybeans closed at $12.78, both sitting above their 52-week highs. Corn at $5.11 barely moved. The heatwave narrative did the work this week, and now the calendar rolls to September WASDE on the 9th, where USDA's first post-tour yield update either confirms the bullish read or hands the funds a reason to exit.
the_takeaway: Wheat and beans earned the week; September WASDE decides whether they keep it.
teaser: Wheat ran 21 cents Friday. Beans set a 52-week high. Corn watched. Here's what it means going into September.

one_number.context: CHS and OCP North America announced the first domestic phosphate fertilizer plant in 40 years, sited in Louisiana. If it gets built, it changes the input-cost conversation for 2028 and beyond; for 2027, the phosphate squeeze is already baked in.

sections.title: WHEAT AND BEANS LEAD THE WEEK
sections.body:
- Chicago wheat closed Friday at **$7.66**, up 21 cents on the session; confirm the 52-week high before calling it broken -- what is clear is the heatwave narrative pulled winter wheat along with the bean complex all week.
- November soybeans finished at **$12.8775**, also testing multi-month highs, with soybean meal up 2.9% on the day as crush demand and heat-driven yield anxiety kept the bid alive.
- Corn at **$5.11** barely moved, down less than 2 cents; December at **$5.3625** held flat, which keeps the pricing window from this week open but not forever.
sections.bottom_line: Wheat and beans did the work this week; corn is along for the ride, not leading it.
sections.farmer_action: December corn at $5.3625: third session this call has been made. Price it or own the risk into September WASDE.

sections.title: CATTLE HOLD; SCREWWORM CLOCK TICKING
sections.body:
- Live cattle closed at **$220.55**, up a tenth of a percent, essentially unchanged; the market is holding but not pushing, exactly where it has been all week with the Cargill multi-plant lockout, ongoing since May 19, still removing roughly 6,000 head of daily processing capacity.
- Feeders at $320.90 slipped half a percent, consistent with the late-July pattern of pricing returning Mexican supply ahead of the Aug 24 Douglas, AZ phased reopening, now in its first week of operation.
- Lean hogs at $81.90 were the livestock complex's best mover Friday, up 1.7%, with no specific news catalyst; looks like position-squaring into the long weekend.
sections.catalyst: Cargill lockout capacity constraint ongoing; Douglas, AZ screwworm port reopening now active as of Aug 24.
sections.bottom_line: Feeders are pricing the reopening, not the scarcity; watch feeder/live spread through September.

sections.title: ENERGY: QATAR FORCE MAJEURE KEEPS HORMUZ PREMIUM ALIVE
sections.body:
- WTI closed at **$83.44**, up 0.4% Friday, a quiet close that understates the week's real energy story: Qatar extended its LNG force majeure through November as Hormuz transit blockages continue, a direct echo of the Iran-Hormuz cycle that re-escalated in early-to-mid July when commercial vessels were hit and tanker traffic reversed course.
- Natural gas at $2.88 slipped 1.4%, with the Qatar LNG story more relevant to Asian and European spot prices than to Henry Hub in the near term.
- Diesel near-record highs, per AgWeb Friday, are the input story that matters most for harvest operations starting in the next two to four weeks; crude's calm close does not mean diesel follows.
sections.catalyst: Qatar extends LNG force majeure through November on Hormuz transit blockage; AgWeb flags diesel near record highs ahead of harvest.
sections.bottom_line: Crude calm, diesel hot; harvest fieldwork cost is the real energy number this week.

sections.title: MACRO: DOLLAR FIRMS, METALS FALL
sections.body:
- The Dollar Index at **$99.68**, up half a percent Friday, is a quiet headwind for any export-driven commodity rally; beans and wheat shrugged it off this week, but a sustained dollar move above $100 would start to compete with the heat premium.
- Gold off 2.7% and silver off 3.6% Friday suggest a risk-off pocket in macro markets that the ag complex ignored; S&P at $7,711 dipped 0.2%, nothing alarming.
- Farm bankruptcy tracking data, released Friday by NASDA and NALC covering Chapter 11 and 12 filings, is the quieter macro story: financial stress in the sector is rising even as board prices are firm, a split that the September WASDE won't resolve.
sections.catalyst: Dollar Index firmed 0.5%; NASDA/NALC new DEBT project publishes farm bankruptcy trend data.
sections.bottom_line: Board prices are high but the stress data says not every producer is capturing them.

outside_the_pit.title: First US Phosphate Plant in 40 Years Planned for Louisiana
outside_the_pit.body: CHS and OCP North America announced a $450 million phosphate fertilizer plant in Louisiana, the first domestic build of its kind in four decades. It won't affect 2027 input costs, but it is the first structural answer to the supply squeeze that Iran-related disruptions have made worse this year.

outside_the_pit.title: NASDA Launches Farm Bankruptcy Tracker as Filings Rise
outside_the_pit.body: NASDA and NALC are now compiling Chapter 11 and 12 agricultural bankruptcy filings in a new database called DEBT. Board prices near multi-year highs have not prevented rising financial distress, especially for producers who locked basis or sold forward below current levels.

the_more_you_know.title: Farm bankruptcies are rising while the board is high. That is not a contradiction.
the_more_you_know.body: The NASDA/NALC DEBT tracker launched Friday to document exactly this: producers who sold forward below today's $12.78 beans or $5.11 corn, or who carry high input-cost debt from 2024-25, are not benefiting from Friday's closes. A high board and rising bankruptcy filings can coexist, and this data set will be the tell going into 2027.

watch_list.desc: Weekly export sales. Beans under 400K MT says the rally is chart-driven, not demand-driven. Above 600K MT extends the bid.
USDA Crop Progress, 3:00 PM CT. Corn condition holding above 60% good/excellent keeps the September WASDE yield cut thesis alive; a drop below 55% adds weather premium.
Watch December corn at $5.36: a close above $5.40 opens the next leg; a fade below $5.25 says the heat premium was already the whole story.

September WASDE, 11:00 AM CT. USDA's first post-tour survey-based update on corn and soybean yields. Corn below 179 bu/acre or beans below 52.0 would extend Friday's rally; above August's 180.7/52.7 hands funds a reason to step back.

daily_quote.text: Failure is simply the opportunity to begin again, this time more intelligently.
